claim: Moving an established statistical analysis between programming languages requires preserving parameter conventions, observation models and numerical behavior. HGFX provides hierarchical Gaussian filtering in Python against a frozen MATLAB HGF Toolbox 8.2.0 reference, without MATLAB in the user runtime. We present the statistical contract, user workflow and scoped evaluation of HGFX 1.0.0. In 36 paired model-selection datasets, the implementations select identical Bayesian information criterion winners, while generating-model recovery balanced accuracy is 0.583 in each. Parameter recovery does not meet all predeclared criteria. A separate trial-horizon experiment fails its integrity gate. Inspection of its retained raw outputs distinguishes ten datasets with no selectable model in either implementation from disagreement between two selected models, and identifies four asymmetric initial-fit outcomes. A mapped comparison with pyhgf 0.3.2 shows agreement for 11 perceptual quantities in one binary case; response likelihood remains not directly comparable. Retained Tesla T4 measurements establish objective agreement in tested cells, without a speed claim. A reproducible continuous-input example uses the reference toolbox's empirical USD/CHF series; customized published participant analyses remain outside the demonstrated application scope. HGFX's contribution is a versioned compatibility workflow with inspectable numerical boundaries. Cross-implementation agreement does not establish parameter identifiability, reliable model discrimination or validity for a new experimental design.

claim: The Hierarchical Gaussian Filter (HGF) describes learning about states whose uncertainty and volatility change over time [@mathys2011; @mathys2014]. The MATLAB implementation associated with TAPAS supplies model configurations, fitting, simulation and diagnostic workflows [@fraessle2021tapas]. These supporting conventions matter to an applied analysis because they determine which quantities are estimated and how the resulting evidence is calculated.

claim: Numerical evaluation adds another layer. The HGF is recursive, so a local discrepancy can propagate through later beliefs. Fitting adds derivatives, optimizer stopping decisions and curvature calculations. Agreement of a fixed-parameter trajectory is therefore necessary evidence for a fitting comparison, but it does not imply identical fitted parameters. Conversely, a fitted endpoint discrepancy does not locate the underlying cause. It may reflect a changed observation model, a different transform, a numerical derivative, or sensitivity within the reference implementation. These possibilities require distinct checks rather than a single correlation between output vectors. General guidance on computational modeling likewise distinguishes implementation checks from recovery and substantive inference [@wilson2019ten], within the broader requirement for computational reproducibility [@peng2011reproducible].

claim: Belief inference and parameter optimization solve different problems. The filter produces a trajectory conditional on parameters; maximum a posteriori optimization searches for parameters using the likelihood and priors. Curvature at the fitted solution then supports the documented approximate covariance and Laplace evidence calculations. Bayesian information criterion (BIC) uses the negative log likelihood, free-parameter count and reference observation count; it is not the negative log joint. The evaluation consequently checks objective components and statistical outputs separately. No new inferential method is proposed here.

claim: The trial-horizon experiment fails its paired-integrity gate. A retrospective audit of the original 24 shard archives clarifies why: all 62 datasets with nonempty selected-model labels agree, while ten datasets have no selected model in either implementation because simulation was invalid. The frozen checker counts these empty pairs as failed winner matches; they are not ten pairs choosing different models. Of 144 parameter cases, 20 share an invalid simulation and four have an HGFX initial-objective rejection with a MATLAB success flag. Two of those MATLAB outputs have nonfinite negative log joint values; the other two return finite values. All 120 successful pairs have the expected free indices. Thus the 24 failed index checks reflect empty failure outputs, not observed parameter-order differences between successful fits. The classifier propagates its global gate failure to all three families, so its labels do not localize a defect to every family. These distinctions correct interpretation without changing the frozen gate, replacing failed data or claiming identifiability. Supplement S3 retains the four asymmetric cases and the limits of their localization.

claim: The continuous-input example applies the released wheel to the entire USD/CHF series distributed with the frozen toolbox. The upstream demo describes exchange rates during 2010 and 2011; the file supplies values without calendar labels. Consequently, the example uses observation number rather than invented dates and treats the series' upstream description as its provenance. It estimates perceptual parameters from the input likelihood, without participant choices or synthetic response measurements. The run completed in 182 seconds on CPU float64, returning negative log likelihood -2387.622 and BIC -4736.724 for 614 observations. A continuous density can exceed one, so a negative negative-log-likelihood is not itself an error. Figure 5 shows the observations and fitted-filter predictions. Parameters were estimated from the full series: the one-step predictions are therefore in-sample diagnostics, not held-out forecasts. Numerical-derivative warnings occurred; finite statistics are not treated as a convergence or curvature-validation certificate. Supplement S6 records the execution and remaining diagnostics.
